plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: Glossy evergreen shrubs light up the cold winter landscape with rose-like blooms. Each flower has layers of satin petals around a boss of golden stamens. Against dark green leaves, and sometimes a dusting of snow, the flowers look bright and almost unreal.
plants.bloomingSeason: Wild plants flower from January to March, so mid-January falls within the season.
plants.location: Coastal woodlands and gardens of Japan, in the Northern Hemisphere's winter
plants.funFact: Camellia japonica is a close relative of the tea plant, Camellia sinensis. Its seeds are pressed to make camellia oil, which has long been used in Japan for hair care and cooking.

plants.name: Agapanthus praecox
plants.description: Tall, bare stems rise from clumps of strappy leaves. Each stem carries a rounded burst of funnel-shaped flowers, like a blue firework. In midsummer gardens the globes sway above the foliage and attract bees.
plants.bloomingSeason: Most flowering runs from November to February, so mid-January is the peak of the Southern Hemisphere summer.
plants.location: Gardens and roadsides in eastern Australia, and native to South Africa
plants.funFact: Despite the common name, it is not a true lily. Its name comes from Greek words meaning 'love flower'. It is also tough enough to have escaped gardens and naturalized in parts of Australia.

plants.name: Helleborus niger
plants.description: This low woodland perennial opens pure white, cup-shaped flowers in the coldest part of the year. They have golden stamens at the center and often age to a blush of pink. They nod above leathery, dark green leaves, and some gardeners find them in the snow.
plants.bloomingSeason: In the southeastern United States it is usually in flower by late December or early January, so it is blooming around January 17.
plants.location: Shaded winter gardens in the temperate Northern Hemisphere, such as North Carolina, USA. Native to the mountains of central and southern Europe.
plants.funFact: Despite its common name, it is not a rose. It belongs to the buttercup family, and all parts of the plant are toxic, which helps keep grazing animals away.
